summary: Describes a minimal mode of operation for IPv6 over the TSCH mode of IEEE 802.15.4e networks. It names the baseline protocols, configurations and modes needed for a functioning 6TiSCH network. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: 6TiSCH is a way of running IPv6 over small radios that take turns on different channels. This document fixes the smallest set of settings that every such device must use, so that they can find each other, join the same network and pass traffic.

questions: how does a node join a 6tisch network
what is an enhanced beacon in tsch
subtitle: The baseline settings every 6TiSCH device needs so tiny, channel-hopping radios can form an IPv6 network and talk to each other.

tldr.problem: Tiny radios that hop between channels need the same settings and the same joining procedure, or they cannot form one working network.
tldr.mechanism: The document fixes the radio schedule, the enhanced beacon that advertises it, the link-layer security keys and the RPL objective function, so that any two compliant devices can join the same network.
tldr.outcome: Interoperable IPv6 connectivity over channel-hopping meshes with a known baseline. RFC 8180 is an Internet Best Current Practice.

today: RFC 8180 is an Internet Best Current Practice, published in May 2017. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so the guidance stands as written.

sections.title: What a 6TiSCH Network Is
sections.content:
A 6TiSCH network gives IPv6 connectivity over a Time-Slotted Channel Hopping mesh, as described in RFC 7554, made of IEEE Std 802.15.4 TSCH links. The IPv6 connectivity comes from the 6LoWPAN framework of RFC 4944, RFC 6282, RFC 8025, RFC 8138 and RFC 6775, together with RPL from RFC 6550 and the RPL Objective Function 0 from RFC 6552.

The specification defines the operational parameters and procedures for a minimal mode of operation, and any compliant device should implement it. The parameter configuration provides the bandwidth the nodes need to bootstrap the network, which covers the initial network configuration and the security bootstrapping. The 802.15.4 TSCH mode, the 6LoWPAN framework, RPL and the objective function are used unmodified. Parameters and particular operations of TSCH are specified so that nodes in the network interoperate.

In a 6TiSCH network, nodes follow the communication schedule of 802.15.4 TSCH and learn it when they join. Under this specification, the learned schedule is the same for every node and does not change over time. Later specifications may define mechanisms for managing the schedule dynamically, but dynamic scheduling is out of scope here. More advanced work is expected to complement the minimal configuration with operations that adapt the schedule to the traffic at run time.
sections.plainLanguage: Small radios cannot listen on every channel at once, so they take turns: one channel for a short slot, then the next. Time Slotted Channel Hopping is that scheme. This document says what settings every device must use so they can agree on when to talk and how to join.

sections.title: The Radio Schedule
sections.content:
An implementation compliant with this specification MUST implement IEEE Std 802.15.4 in Time-Slotted Channel Hopping mode. Where this specification and the IEEE standard disagree, the IEEE standard takes precedence. The properties marked in the EB column of the recommended settings table are announced in the enhanced beacons the nodes send, and are learned by those joining the network, so changing their value means changing the contents of the beacon.

The recommended settings are: a tunable slotframe size, which trades bandwidth against energy; one scheduled cell, at timeslot 0x0000 and channel offset 0x0000, with link options setting TX Link, RX Link, Shared Link and Timekeeping; all the remaining cells in the slotframe unscheduled; a maximum of 3 link-layer retransmissions, giving 4 transmission attempts; the default timeslot template, macTimeslotTemplateId of 0; a tunable enhanced beacon period, which trades joining time against energy; the default number of used frequencies, 16, for the 2.4 GHz O-QPSK physical layer; and the default channel hopping sequence, macHoppingSequenceID of 0.

This minimal mode uses a single slotframe made of a tunable number of timeslots. The size needs to be tuned, and how to tune it is out of scope. The slotframe size is announced in the beacon, and the recommended value for the slotframe handle is 0x00. An implementation MAY use a different handle, for example to add other slotframes with higher priority, though that is out of scope here.

There is a single scheduled cell, which MAY sit at any slot and channel offset in the slotframe. Its position is announced in the beacon and its LinkType is ADVERTISING, so that beacons can be sent on it. The document shows an example slotframe of 101 timeslots, which gives a radio duty cycle below 0.99%.

A node MAY use the scheduled cell to send and receive every kind of link-layer frame. Beacons go to the link-layer broadcast address and are not acknowledged, while data frames are sent as unicast and are acknowledged by the receiving neighbour. In the scheduled cell a node transmits if it has a packet to send and listens otherwise, so both the TX and RX bits are set. When it transmits and asks for a link-layer acknowledgement but does not receive one, it uses a back-off to resolve a possible collision, so the Shared bit is set. A joining node keeps time synchronised to its initial time-source neighbour using that cell, so the Timekeeping bit is set. The resulting link option sets TX Link, RX Link, Shared Link and Timekeeping to 1, and clears Priority and the three reserved bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The schedule is one repeating frame of timeslots with a single cell where traffic is actually sent. Everything else stays quiet, which is what keeps the radios from using much energy. The cell's position and size are announced in the beacon, so a joining device copies them.

sections.title: Joining and the Enhanced Beacon
sections.content:
After booting, a node starts in an unsynchronized, unjoined state and achieves initial synchronisation by listening for enhanced beacons. It may hear beacons from several networks, and the mechanisms for telling them apart are out of scope.

The IEEE standard does not define how often beacons are sent or what they contain. In a minimal TSCH configuration a node SHOULD send a beacon every EB_PERIOD, and tuning that period trades joining time against energy. Beacons are used to learn about local networks and to synchronise the absolute slot number and the time offset of the network the node decides to join. Once joined, a node MAY keep listening for beacons to gather information about other networks. During joining, before secure connections to the time parents exist, a node MAY maintain synchronisation using beacons.

The IEEE standard requires beacons so that nodes can join, and they SHOULD carry these information elements:

  • The TSCH Synchronization IE, holding synchronisation information such as the absolute slot number and the Join Metric, which gives the topological distance between the node sending the beacon and the PAN coordinator.
  • The TSCH Timeslot IE, holding the timeslot template identifier that specifies the internal timing of the timeslot; the default template is recommended.
  • The Channel Hopping IE, holding the channel hopping sequence identifier; the default sequence is recommended.
  • The TSCH Slotframe and Link IE, which lets joining nodes learn the initial schedule; a single cell is recommended.

A node that follows the recommended settings exactly sends a beacon with the same contents as the one it received when it joined, except for the Join Metric field in the TSCH Synchronization IE. Once a node has joined a network and configured its schedule this way, it SHOULD ignore later beacons that would change the configured parameters, though it may still listen to beacons from other networks.

The 802.15.4 header details are also fixed. The Frame Version field MUST be set to 0b10, and the Sequence Number field MAY be elided. The beacon destination address MUST be 0xFFFF, the short broadcast address, and the beacon source address SHOULD be the node's short address if that is supported, otherwise the long address. The PAN ID Compression bit SHOULD indicate that the source PAN ID is not present and the destination PAN ID is present.
sections.plainLanguage: A new device boots up and listens. It hears a beacon that tells it the time, the schedule and how far away the network root is, and it copies those settings. Later beacons that would change the schedule are ignored, so the network does not wobble.

sections.title: RPL Settings
sections.content:
In a multi-hop topology the RPL routing protocol MAY be used. If it is, nodes MUST implement the RPL Objective Function Zero, and the rank of a node is computed as the rank of its parent plus a rank increment, where the increment is (Rf times Sp plus Sr) multiplied by the minimum hop rank increase. The objective function parameters that MUST be used are Rf of 1, Sp of (3 times ETX) minus 2, Sr of 0, a minimum hop rank increase of 256, a minimum step of rank of 1, a maximum step of rank of 9, and an ETX limit for selecting a parent of 3.

The step of rank uses the Expected Transmission Count. An implementation MUST follow the normalization guidance of the objective function, and Sp SHOULD be calculated as (3 times ETX) minus 2. The minimum value of Sp indicates a good quality link and the maximum a poor one, with the default indicating an average one. Candidate parents with an ETX greater than 3 SHOULD NOT be selected, which avoids having ETX values on used links larger than the maximum allowed number of transmission attempts.

The worked example uses a five-hop network where the number of transmissions is 100 and the number of acknowledgements is 75 on every link, giving a rank increment of 512. The ranks are then 256 at the root, then 768, 1280, 1792, 2304 and 2816, and the DAG ranks are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11.

When RPL is used, nodes MUST implement the non-storing mode of operation. The storing mode SHOULD be implemented by nodes with enough capabilities, and nodes that do not implement RPL MUST join as leaf nodes. RPL signalling messages such as DODAG Information Objects are sent using the Trickle algorithm with the RPL-defined default values.

RPL information and hop-by-hop extension headers MUST follow RFC 6553 and RFC 6554. For packets that need to cross intermediate routers they MUST follow the IP-in-IP encapsulation requirement of RFC 6282 and RFC 2460. Routing extension headers such as the RPL Packet Information and the Source Routing Header, and outer IP headers where there is encapsulation, MUST be compressed according to RFC 8138 and RFC 8025.
sections.plainLanguage: Where the network is more than one hop across, RPL builds the routes. The document fixes one ranking rule, so every node computes the same view of the network, and it fixes the Trickle timer settings so that routing updates keep a predictable rhythm.

sections.title: Network Formation and Lifetime
sections.content:
The Join Metric in the TSCH Synchronization IE of the beacon MUST be calculated from the routing metric of the node and normalised to a value between 0 and 255. A lower Join Metric means the beacon sender is topologically closer to the root of the network, and so a joining node should prefer to synchronise to it.

Where the network uses RPL, the Join Metric of every node, including the DAG root, MUST be set to the DAG rank minus one. Since the DAG rank of the root's rank is 1, the root's Join Metric is 0, which matches the 802.15.4 requirement that the root use a Join Metric of 0. Where the network does not use RPL, the Join Metric follows the rules of the IEEE standard.

When a node joins, it may hear beacons from several nodes already in the network, and which neighbour to synchronise to, that is, which becomes the initial time-source neighbour, is implementation specific. For example, after the first beacon a node MAY listen for at most MAX_EB_DELAY seconds, waiting for beacons from NUM_NEIGHBOURS_TO_WAIT distinct neighbours, and MAY then use the Join Metric in each beacon to pick the time-source neighbour. At all times a node MUST maintain synchronisation to at least one time-source neighbour, and that neighbour MUST be chosen from the neighbours in the RPL routing parent set where RPL is used. A node that cannot keep contact with at least one time-source neighbour loses synchronisation and has to join the network again.

A RPL node that joins the network MUST NOT send beacons before it has acquired a RPL rank, so that the time synchronisation structure stays consistent, and the same applies to other routing protocols with their own metrics. Once it has acquired routing information it SHOULD start sending beacons.

To avoid constant changes of parent when ranks are compared, a boundary value, the parent switch threshold, is recommended. When a candidate parent belongs to a smaller path cost than the current minimum path, the candidate is selected only if the difference between the new path and the current path is greater than the threshold, otherwise the node MAY keep the current preferred parent. The threshold SHOULD be 192 when the ETX metric is used, in the form 128 times ETX, and the recommendation for this document is 640 when the metric is ((3 times ETX) minus 2) times the minimum hop rank increase, or a proportional value. This covers hysteresis for both routing parent and time-source neighbour selection.
sections.plainLanguage: Every beacon carries a number saying how close the sender is to the root, so a joining device can pick the best neighbour to follow for timing. A node must keep at least one such neighbour, and it only changes parents when the improvement is clearly worth it, which stops the routing flapping.

sections.title: Implementation Recommendations
sections.content:
The format of the neighbour table is implementation specific, but the recommended per-neighbour information is: an identifier for the neighbour, such as an EUI-64; the number of link-layer transmission attempts to that neighbour; the number of transmitted link-layer frames that neighbour acknowledged; the number of link-layer frames received from that neighbour; a timestamp of when the last frame was received, based on the absolute slot number or any other time base, which can trigger a keep-alive; the routing metric for that neighbour, for example its RPL rank; and a flag saying whether the neighbour is a time-source neighbour.

The 802.15.4 standard does not define the use of queues for upper-layer data, so the following rules are recommended. A node keeps a configurable number of upper-layer packets per link in its queues, the default being NUM_UPPERLAYER_PACKETS, for a configurable time that should cover the joining process, the default being MAX_JOIN_TIME. Frames generated by the 802.15.4 layer, including beacons, are queued with a higher priority than frames from higher layers, and a BEACON frame is queued with a higher priority than a DATA frame.

The recommended settings are MAX_EB_DELAY of 180, NUM_NEIGHBOURS_TO_WAIT of 2, PARENT_SWITCH_THRESHOLD of 640, NUM_UPPERLAYER_PACKETS of 1 and MAX_JOIN_TIME of 300.
sections.plainLanguage: The document also recommends what a device should remember about each neighbour, how it should queue packets while it is joining, and the default numbers for those timers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document is concerned only with link-layer security. Many Internet of Things networks have nodes in physically vulnerable places, so it should be assumed that nodes will be physically compromised, their memories examined and their keys extracted. Fixed secrets will not remain secret, which affects the joining process. Provisioning a network with a fixed link key K2 is not secure, so for most applications there will be a joining phase in which some level of authorisation is allowed for nodes that have not been authenticated. The details are out of scope, but the link layer must provide some flexibility there.

Link-layer frames MUST be secured by the link-layer security mechanisms of the IEEE standard. Authentication MUST be applied to the entire frame, including the 802.15.4 header, and encryption MAY be applied to the payload information elements and the payload. Two keys are assumed: K1 authenticates beacons, which MUST be authenticated only and not encrypted, and K2 authenticates and encrypts data and acknowledgement frames. The keys can be pre-configured or learned in a key distribution phase, and the key distribution mechanisms are out of scope.

What a joining node does depends on which keys it holds. With both K1 and K2 pre-configured it does not rely on a key distribution phase to learn either. With K1 pre-configured but not K2 it authenticates beacons with K1 and relies on the distribution phase to learn K2. With neither, it accepts beacons under the rule in the IEEE standard, that they are passed forward even when the unsecuring process reported an error, and then runs the key distribution phase to learn both keys, with the node it talks to using the security exemption mechanism for frames from the joining node and clearing those exemptions once the phase is done. On a network reset, the new network MUST either use new cryptographic keys or ensure that the absolute slot number keeps increasing.

If an attacker obtains K1 it can generate fake beacons and attack a whole network by sending authenticated beacons, and can make a joining node start joining towards the attacker. If the joining process includes authentication and the distribution of K2 the joining node will notice the attack and fail. If K2 is compromised as well, the node will not notice and the network is compromised. An attacker who knows neither key can still send beacons authenticated with an arbitrary key. With K1 pre-configured, the joining node can tell the fake beacons apart and they have no effect. With neither key pre-configured, the node may mistake a fake beacon for a real one and start joining towards the attacker, but that joining process will fail, since the node cannot authenticate the attacker during the security handshake, and it will have to start listening for beacons again. The node never joins the attacker, but the attempt costs it time and energy, which is an attack in its own right.

The absolute slot number provides a nonce for the security operations in a slot, and any reuse of it with a given key exposes information about encrypted packet contents and risks replay attacks. Replay is prevented because on a network reset either new keys are used or the absolute slot number keeps increasing.

Accurate time synchronisation is critical, so timing information from unsecured sources MUST be avoided during normal operation. During joining a node may be susceptible to timing attacks before it has learned K1 and K2. Denying-of-service attacks at the MAC layer in a low-power network are easy to achieve with radio jamming, and that is the base case against which more sophisticated attacks should be judged. For example, sending fake beacons announcing a very low Join Metric may make a node waste time and energy trying to join a fake network even while legitimate beacons are being heard. Proper join security stops the node from joining the false network, but by then the time and energy are gone.

The 6TiSCH layer SHOULD keep track of anomalous events and report them to a higher authority. For example, beacons reporting low Join Metrics for networks that cannot be joined may be a sign of attack. In normal operation, message integrity check failures on packets with a valid cyclic redundancy check will occur at a rate on the order of once per million packets, and any significant deviation from that rate may be a sign of a network attack, as may time updates in acknowledgements or beacons that are inconsistent with the node's own sense of time and its plausible drift rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices in the field can be opened and their keys read, so the joining procedure has to cope with that. Beacons are signed with one key and data with another, and the document explains what an attacker can do with each key and how the join procedure should react.
